topic: The spotlight effect: nobody's watching you as much as you think
title: Nobody's Watching You As Much As You Think
voiceover: Do you think everyone noticed that mistake? Psychologists call this the spotlight effect: feeling like you're on stage when you're actually in the audience. In 2000, Thomas Gilovich and colleagues had students wear an embarrassing Barry Manilow T-shirt into a room of other students. The wearers guessed about half the people would notice it. Only around a quarter actually did. Why? You're the star of your own experience, so your flaws feel huge. Everyone else is busy starring in theirs. Your own embarrassment feels loud, but other people can't hear it. Before your next big moment, ask: if I saw this happen to someone else, would I remember it tomorrow? Probably not. Then go ahead and take the stage. Tomorrow: the sneaky reason a price ending in nine feels so much cheaper.

description: Think everyone noticed your slip-up? In a classic study, people wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about twice as many observers would notice it as actually did. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000), 'The spotlight effect in social judgment', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
accuracy_note: Figures are approximate: in the original study wearers estimated roughly 46% of observers would notice the shirt, versus roughly 23% who did. The effect has been replicated across several tasks, but sizes vary.
